title: A cosmic unit
question: An astronomer says a star is 4 light-years away. What kind of quantity is a light-year?
choices: Distance
Time
Brightness
explanation: A light-year is the distance light travels through a vacuum in one year. It is a unit of distance, even though its name contains a unit of time.

title: A star in the telescope
question: Light from a star takes 100 years to reach Earth. When you observe that light, what are you seeing?
choices: The star exactly as it is now
The star as it will be in 100 years
The star as it was about 100 years ago
explanation: Light has a finite travel time. The light arriving now left the star roughly a century ago, so the image carries information about that earlier time.

title: A signal from the Moon
question: If the Moon changed abruptly, would an observer on Earth see the change at exactly the same instant?
choices: Only if the Moon is full
No: its light takes time to travel
Yes: light has no travel time
explanation: Light takes a little over a second to travel from the Moon to Earth. Even nearby astronomical views show the object slightly in the past.

title: A ray from the Sun
question: When sunlight reaches Earth, which is true about when it left the Sun?
choices: It left several minutes earlier
It left at that exact instant
It left several years earlier
explanation: Sunlight takes about eight minutes to travel from the Sun to Earth. Looking at the Sun is therefore seeing the surface as it was minutes earlier.

title: A boundary of visibility
question: What does the boundary of the observable universe describe?
choices: A physical wall at the edge of all space
The outer edge of the Milky Way
A limit to what light has had time to reach us
explanation: The observable universe is limited by the light and other signals that have been able to reach us during cosmic history. That boundary is not known to be a physical wall.

title: Two cosmic viewpoints
question: Would observers in very distant galaxies necessarily have exactly the same observable region as Earth?
choices: No: only Earth has an observable region
No: their observable regions are centered on their locations
Yes: every observer sees exactly the same region
explanation: Each observer has a region from which signals could have reached them. Different locations have different observable regions, although those regions can overlap.

title: Nested cosmic structures
question: Which arrangement correctly places our cosmic home?
choices: Solar System inside the Milky Way, inside the universe
Milky Way inside the Solar System
The universe inside the Milky Way
explanation: The Solar System is part of the Milky Way galaxy, and the Milky Way is one galaxy in the universe. These structures differ enormously in scale.

title: A deep field of galaxies
question: For distant galaxies, why does looking farther away usually mean looking further back in cosmic history?
choices: Distant galaxies are always intrinsically younger today
Telescopes can reverse time
Their light generally spent longer traveling to us
explanation: Light from more distant galaxies generally takes longer to reach us. We see those galaxies at earlier stages, rather than seeing their present appearance directly.

title: A very long light trip
question: Can the current distance to a very distant galaxy exceed the time its light traveled multiplied by the speed of light?
choices: Only if light traveled faster than light
Yes: cosmic expansion changes distances during the trip
No: all cosmic distances are fixed during the trip
explanation: In an expanding universe, distances between widely separated galaxies can change while light is traveling. The present distance is therefore not always the travel time multiplied by light speed.

title: Two cosmic neighborhoods
question: Which is the larger structure: the Milky Way or the Solar System?
choices: The Milky Way
The Solar System
They are the same size
explanation: The Milky Way contains the Sun and its Solar System along with many other stars and planetary systems. A galaxy is a much larger structure than one solar system.

title: Beyond the rainbow
question: Which radiation can a telescope detect even though it is outside ordinary human vision?
choices: Infrared light
Only visible green light
No electromagnetic radiation
explanation: Visible light is only one part of the electromagnetic spectrum. Telescopes can be designed to detect infrared, radio, X-ray and other wavelengths that our eyes cannot see.

title: A cloud becomes clearer
question: Why can infrared observations reveal some objects hidden by cosmic dust in visible-light images?
choices: Infrared destroys all cosmic dust
Infrared makes all stars disappear
Some infrared wavelengths pass through dust more effectively
explanation: Dust blocks and scatters visible light strongly in many regions. Some infrared wavelengths pass through those clouds more effectively, revealing features otherwise obscured.

title: A stretched wave
question: A spectral line is observed at a longer wavelength than it was emitted. What is this change called?
choices: Polarization
Redshift
Blueshift
explanation: Redshift means light is observed at longer wavelengths than its emitted wavelength. Cosmological expansion is one way to produce such a shift in distant galaxies.

title: A compressed wave
question: A spectral line is observed at a shorter wavelength than it was emitted. What is this change called?
choices: Blueshift
Redshift
Absorption
explanation: Blueshift means a shift toward shorter wavelengths. It can arise when a source and observer approach each other; not every galaxy is receding locally.

title: Reading starlight
question: How can a spectrum help identify an element in a star?
choices: Every element produces the same line pattern
The star must be sampled directly
Its pattern of spectral lines acts as a fingerprint
explanation: Atoms and ions absorb or emit light at characteristic wavelengths. Comparing the pattern of lines with laboratory spectra helps identify chemical elements.

title: A glowing gas spectrum
question: A hot, thin gas emits light at particular wavelengths. What can appear in its spectrum?
choices: A single line shared by all elements
Bright emission lines
Only a featureless black image
explanation: Excited atoms can emit photons at characteristic wavelengths. A thin glowing gas can therefore produce bright emission lines rather than an entirely continuous spectrum.

title: A spectrum through gas
question: What can produce dark absorption lines in an otherwise continuous spectrum?
choices: Cooler gas absorbing specific wavelengths
A telescope removing every wavelength equally
The absence of atoms anywhere along the light path
explanation: When light passes through suitable cooler gas, atoms can absorb particular wavelengths. Those wavelengths appear as dark lines in a continuous spectrum.

title: Waves and frequency
question: For electromagnetic waves in a vacuum, what happens to frequency when wavelength becomes longer?
choices: Frequency increases
Frequency stays fixed
Frequency decreases
explanation: In a vacuum, wavelength multiplied by frequency equals the speed of light. If wavelength increases, frequency decreases so that their product remains constant.

title: Color and energy
question: How does the energy of a photon change when its frequency increases?
choices: It stays the same
It increases
It decreases
explanation: A photon's energy is proportional to its frequency. Higher-frequency electromagnetic radiation has more energy per photon than lower-frequency radiation.

title: One sky, many views
question: Why do astronomers observe the same object at several wavelengths?
choices: Different wavelengths can reveal different physical features
Every wavelength always shows identical details
A single wavelength measures every property
explanation: Objects emit, absorb and scatter different wavelengths in different ways. Comparing observations across the spectrum can reveal structures and processes a single band misses.

title: Distant galaxy pairs
question: In the standard expanding-universe model, what happens to the separation between distant galaxies carried with the expansion?
choices: Their separation increases
Every galaxy must move through space from one central point
Atoms necessarily expand with the universe
explanation: On sufficiently large scales, cosmic expansion increases the distance between galaxies that follow the overall flow. Gravitationally bound systems do not simply expand with that flow.

title: A question of viewpoint
question: In a homogeneous expanding-space model, which galaxy is the unique center of the expansion?
choices: The Milky Way
The brightest galaxy
There is no special central galaxy
explanation: In the ideal homogeneous model, each observer sees distant galaxies recede on large scales. The model does not assign a unique central galaxy within space.

title: The Solar System and space
question: Does cosmic expansion force the Solar System to expand along with distant intergalactic space?
choices: Only during the daytime
No: local binding dominates at this scale
Yes: every orbit expands at the cosmic rate
explanation: The Solar System is gravitationally bound. Local forces dominate there, so the expansion seen between widely separated galaxies does not simply stretch planetary orbits.

title: A wave crosses expanding space
question: What can happen to a photon's wavelength while it travels through expanding space?
choices: Its wavelength is stretched
It must always become shorter
It becomes a sound wave
explanation: As space expands during a photon's journey, the observed wavelength can be stretched. This cosmological redshift is a key clue to the expansion history.

title: Two gaps on a grid
question: In a uniform-expansion model, both gaps grow by the same factor. Which gap gains more absolute distance?
choices: The initially smaller gap
Both gain the same absolute distance
The initially larger gap
explanation: When every separation is multiplied by the same scale factor, a larger initial separation has a larger absolute increase. The proportional change is the same for both gaps.

title: The balloon analogy
question: What important limitation should you remember when using a balloon surface to picture cosmic expansion?
choices: Galaxies must be rubber dots
The surface represents space; the surrounding room is not required by the model
The universe must have a balloon center inside ordinary space
explanation: A balloon's surface can illustrate distances growing without a special center on that surface. The surrounding room is a feature of the analogy, not an established external space required by cosmology.

title: Why lines move redward
question: A distant galaxy's familiar spectral lines arrive shifted toward longer wavelengths. What can the shift help astronomers study?
choices: Cosmic expansion since the light was emitted
Only the galaxy's chemical color
The number of planets in the Milky Way
explanation: Astronomers compare observed spectral lines with laboratory wavelengths. Cosmological redshift gives information about how much the universe expanded while the light traveled.

title: A common growth factor
question: In a simple expansion model, what does the scale factor describe?
choices: The physical size of every atom
The temperature of an individual star
How cosmic distances in the model change over time
explanation: The cosmological scale factor tracks how distances between idealized comoving points change over time. It is a property of the model's large-scale geometry.

title: Growth is not acceleration
question: What is the difference between cosmic expansion and accelerated expansion?
choices: Acceleration means all galaxies are slowing locally
Acceleration means the expansion rate of a given separation increases over time
They mean exactly the same thing
explanation: Expansion means cosmic scale grows. Accelerated expansion adds a further claim: the scale factor's rate of increase grows over time, as inferred from observations.

title: A nearby exception
question: Must every nearby galaxy recede from the Milky Way because the universe expands on large scales?
choices: No: local gravitational motions can dominate
Yes: every galaxy always recedes
No: galaxies never move
explanation: The overall expansion describes large-scale behavior. Nearby galaxies can have local motions caused by gravity; for example, local approaches are possible.

title: The early-universe model
question: What does the hot Big Bang model describe about the early universe?
choices: It was much hotter and denser
It began as galaxies expanding into an empty room
It began with the present-day distribution of stars
explanation: The hot Big Bang model describes an early universe that was much hotter and denser than today. Its expansion and cooling explain several observations, including the microwave background.

title: The early temperature
question: As the early universe expanded, what happened to its temperature overall?
choices: It stayed exactly constant forever
It rose indefinitely
It fell
explanation: The early universe expanded and cooled. As conditions changed, different particles and eventually atoms could persist, leading to later changes in how light traveled.

title: The earliest nuclei
question: Which nuclei formed in significant amounts during primordial nucleosynthesis?
choices: Complete atoms of every element
Mostly hydrogen and helium nuclei
Iron and uranium nuclei as the main products
explanation: During the first few minutes, nuclear reactions produced mostly hydrogen and helium nuclei, with small amounts of other light nuclei. Heavy elements formed largely through later stellar processes.

title: Nuclei without atoms
question: Why did stable neutral atoms form later than the first light nuclei?
choices: The universe had to cool enough for electrons to remain bound
Electrons did not exist until galaxies formed
Nuclei and neutral atoms always formed simultaneously
explanation: Light nuclei formed while the universe was still extremely hot. Later cooling made it possible for electrons to remain bound to nuclei as neutral atoms.

title: When light traveled freely
question: Why did the early universe become much more transparent after neutral atoms formed?
choices: All photons were destroyed
Space stopped expanding
Photons scattered less often from free electrons
explanation: Before neutral atoms formed, free electrons frequently scattered photons. Once many electrons combined with nuclei, photons traveled much more freely through the universe.

title: The oldest light's snapshot
question: Approximately when was the cosmic microwave background released?
choices: Only after the Milky Way formed
About 380,000 years after the Big Bang
At the formation of Earth
explanation: The cosmic microwave background comes from an early period roughly 380,000 years after the Big Bang, when the universe cooled enough for light to travel much more freely.

title: Two cosmic milestones
question: Which came first in the standard cosmic timeline?
choices: The release of the cosmic microwave background
The formation of the first stars
The formation of the Solar System
explanation: The cosmic microwave background was released before the first stars formed. The intervening period is often called the cosmic dark ages because stars had not yet lit the universe.

title: A chapter before dawn
question: What does the phrase cosmic dark ages refer to?
choices: A time when all radiation disappeared
A present-day region inside Earth's shadow
A period before the first stars illuminated the universe
explanation: After the microwave background was released and before the first stars formed, there were no stars to illuminate the universe. Radiation still existed, including the background light.

title: Light changes gas again
question: What is cosmic reionization?
choices: The cooling of Earth's oceans
The ionization of much intergalactic gas by early sources of radiation
The first formation of neutral atoms
explanation: Radiation from early stars, galaxies and other sources ionized much of the intergalactic gas after neutral atoms had formed. The details and timing are studied with observations.

title: An idea about the earliest expansion
question: What is cosmic inflation in modern cosmology?
choices: A proposed very early period of rapid expansion
The increase in prices on Earth
The formation of the first planets
explanation: Inflation is a proposed period of extremely rapid early expansion. It can explain several large-scale features, but its physical mechanism and details remain under investigation.

title: Looking for a glow
question: Where do astronomers observe the cosmic microwave background?
choices: Across the sky
Only inside the Milky Way
Only around the Sun
explanation: The cosmic microwave background is observed in every direction as a nearly uniform microwave glow. Foreground sources must be separated from the cosmic signal.

title: A map of the microwave sky
question: How uniform is the cosmic microwave background temperature across the sky?
choices: Perfectly identical in every measured direction
Randomly different by thousands of degrees
Nearly uniform, with tiny variations
explanation: The microwave background has nearly the same temperature in all directions, with very small variations. Those variations contain information about the early universe.

title: Seeds in a map
question: Why are tiny variations in the cosmic microwave background scientifically useful?
choices: They prove every galaxy was already fully formed
They reveal small early-universe differences linked to later structure
They are photographs of present-day planets
explanation: Small differences in the early universe are related to the later growth of cosmic structure. Detailed CMB patterns help scientists test models of that evolution.

title: A shell in the sky
question: Is the cosmic microwave background an image of a physical wall at the edge of space?
choices: No: it is light from an early epoch reaching us from many directions
Yes: it is a wall surrounding the universe
No: it is light emitted by the Moon
explanation: The CMB is radiation released when the early universe became transparent. Its apparent sky pattern comes from the early universe along our past light paths, not a physical wall.

title: A cooled glow
question: Why is the cosmic microwave background observed today at microwave wavelengths?
choices: The radiation was created by microwave ovens
The light has never changed wavelength
Expansion stretched the original radiation's wavelengths
explanation: As the universe expanded, the wavelength of the early radiation stretched. The once much hotter radiation is now observed as a cool microwave background.

title: Taking the sky temperature
question: About how warm is the cosmic microwave background today?
choices: Exactly zero kelvin
About 2.7 kelvin
About 270 kelvin
explanation: The cosmic microwave background is observed at a temperature of about 2.7 kelvin. It is cold, but it is not at absolute zero.

title: A snapshot of an epoch
question: What does a map of the cosmic microwave background primarily show?
choices: Conditions when early radiation began traveling freely
A live map of present-day galaxies
The surface of the Sun today
explanation: The CMB carries information from the era when light decoupled from matter in the early universe. It is a snapshot of that distant past, not a live map of today's sky objects.
after: A view of the early cosmos

title: Cleaning the sky map
question: Why must scientists account for foreground emission when studying the CMB?
choices: The CMB occurs only in front of the Moon
Foregrounds make the universe stop expanding
Our galaxy and other sources add signals to the sky
explanation: Microwave observations contain signals from the Milky Way and other foreground sources in addition to the CMB. Analysis attempts to separate these contributions.

title: From faint patterns to galaxies
question: How are early density differences related to the cosmic web?
choices: They erased all differences forever
Gravity helped small differences grow into larger structures
They guaranteed galaxies were present at the CMB epoch
explanation: Small early density differences grew under gravity over cosmic time. This growth contributed to the large-scale distribution of galaxies and clusters observed today.

title: Testing an early-universe idea
question: What can patterns in the CMB help scientists do with inflation models?
choices: Test predictions and constrain models
Prove every detail of inflation's mechanism is known
Directly photograph the instant of the Big Bang
explanation: The CMB's detailed patterns provide tests of predictions from early-universe models, including inflation. The physical mechanism of inflation remains an open research question.

title: A missing light source?
question: Why is dark matter called dark?
choices: It does not emit or absorb light in the ordinary way we detect
It is ordinary dust painted black
It is simply a region with no gravity
explanation: Dark matter is inferred mainly through gravitational effects rather than ordinary emitted or absorbed light. Its underlying particle or physical nature remains unknown.

title: A galaxy's outer stars
question: Why did galaxy rotation measurements become evidence for unseen mass?
choices: Outer stars have no gravity
Galaxies have no stars outside their centers
Outer stars move faster than expected from visible matter alone
explanation: Observed rotation patterns in galaxies indicate more gravitational mass than the visible matter alone accounts for in standard models. Dark matter is a leading explanation.

title: A distant source and mass
question: What is gravitational lensing?
choices: A galaxy switching off its light
The deflection of light by mass along its path
A telescope lens manufactured in space
explanation: Mass curves spacetime and can deflect light from a more distant source. The resulting distortions help astronomers infer the mass distribution of a foreground lens.

title: An invisible mass map
question: How can gravitational lensing help map dark matter?
choices: The distortion of background light reveals intervening mass
It directly photographs dark matter particles
It measures only the brightness of nearby stars
explanation: Lensing reveals mass through its effect on background light, including mass that emits little or no light. It does not by itself identify the particle nature of dark matter.

title: A heavy cluster
question: Why do galaxy clusters provide evidence for additional unseen mass?
choices: Their galaxies contain no stars
Clusters cannot be affected by gravity
Their motions and lensing indicate more mass than visible material alone
explanation: Cluster dynamics and gravitational lensing can reveal gravitational mass beyond the mass inferred from visible matter alone. These are independent ways to investigate the mass budget.

title: Two kinds of matter
question: How does dark matter differ from ordinary luminous matter in astronomical observations?
choices: It has no gravitational effect
It is primarily inferred through gravitational effects
It is made entirely of visible stars
explanation: Ordinary matter can emit, absorb or scatter light. Dark matter is detected mainly through gravity, while its exact composition remains an open question.

title: Two different mysteries
question: What is a key distinction between dark matter and dark energy?
choices: Dark matter clusters gravitationally; dark energy is associated with accelerated expansion
Both are simply names for ordinary stars
Dark matter causes all light and dark energy is moonlight
explanation: Dark matter helps explain gravitational effects in galaxies and larger structures. Dark energy is the name for whatever accounts for the observed accelerated cosmic expansion.

title: The galaxy and its halo
question: In a common galaxy model, where is much of the dark matter?
choices: Only in the galaxy's bright center
Only inside individual stars
In an extended halo around the visible galaxy
explanation: Many galaxy models place dark matter in an extended halo that surrounds the luminous disk. Rotation and other gravitational observations help constrain that distribution.

title: Building the cosmic web
question: What role does dark matter play in standard models of structure formation?
choices: It replaces the need for gravity
Its gravity helps structure grow
It prevents all galaxies from forming
explanation: In standard cosmological models, dark matter contributes gravity that helps matter collect into the large-scale structures in which galaxies form. Observations test these models.

title: An unanswered question
question: Do measurements of dark matter's gravitational effects already establish exactly what it is made of?
choices: No: its physical nature remains unknown
Yes: it is proven to be ordinary smoke
Yes: it is known to be black paint
explanation: Several lines of evidence constrain the gravitational behavior of dark matter. Those measurements have not yet settled the nature of the underlying physical substance.

title: A changing expansion
question: What does accelerated cosmic expansion mean?
choices: The universe's scale factor grows at an increasing rate
The universe has stopped expanding
Every galaxy is accelerating through its local space in the same way
explanation: Accelerated expansion means the cosmic scale factor's rate of increase is growing over time. It is a statement about large-scale expansion, not every object's local motion.

title: A dimmer explosion
question: How did distant Type Ia supernova observations contribute to the discovery of accelerated expansion?
choices: They proved every supernova has the same brightness without correction
They showed that redshift never occurs
They helped measure distances that were greater than expected in a nonaccelerating model
explanation: Standardized Type Ia supernova brightness provides distance estimates. Their distances and redshifts were evidence that cosmic expansion has accelerated in the recent universe.

title: A name for a mystery
question: What does the term dark energy name?
choices: The same thing as the Milky Way's dust
The unknown cause or description associated with accelerated expansion
A directly identified particle emitted by every star
explanation: Dark energy is a name for the phenomenon or component associated with accelerated expansion. Its physical nature is not yet established, and several explanations are investigated.

title: A constant possibility
question: What is a cosmological constant in cosmological modeling?
choices: A constant term compatible with a vacuum-energy-like contribution
A measurement proving space never expands
A constant number of galaxies in every telescope image
explanation: A cosmological constant is a term in Einstein's equations that can behave like a constant vacuum-energy density. It is one possible description of dark energy.

title: Can the cause change?
question: Do observations already prove exactly what dark energy is?
choices: Yes: it is known to be ordinary dust
Yes: its cause was photographed directly
No: its physical nature remains uncertain
explanation: Several observations support accelerated expansion, but its underlying physical explanation remains uncertain. Models include a cosmological constant and alternatives that scientists test.

title: Competing influences
question: Can gravity gather matter into galaxies while the universe expands on large scales?
choices: No: gravity only acts inside stars
Yes: gravity can bind local structures even as large-scale space expands
No: expansion forbids all gravitational structures
explanation: Cosmic expansion describes the large-scale evolution of space. Gravity can nevertheless bind galaxies, clusters and other local structures under suitable conditions.

title: The universe's future
question: Why is the far future of cosmic expansion uncertain?
choices: It depends on the properties of dark energy and the cosmological model
The universe has no measurable expansion history
The future is fixed by the Moon's orbit
explanation: Different assumptions about dark energy and gravity lead to different possible long-term expansion histories. Better measurements help distinguish those possibilities.

title: Matter in a changing volume
question: In a simple model with a fixed amount of ordinary matter, what happens to its average density as space expands?
choices: It increases because volume grows
It stays fixed no matter how much volume grows
It decreases as the same matter occupies more volume
explanation: For a fixed quantity of matter, density is mass divided by volume. As the volume of an expanding region increases, its average matter density falls.

title: An expanding-universe model
question: In the cosmological-constant model, how does its energy density behave as the universe expands?
choices: It is converted into stars at a fixed rate
It remains constant
It falls exactly like ordinary matter density
explanation: In the cosmological-constant model, the associated energy density stays constant as space expands. This is a model property, not proof of dark energy's physical nature.

title: Checking the acceleration
question: Why do cosmologists combine supernova measurements with other observations?
choices: Different probes test expansion and structure with different uncertainties
One supernova determines every cosmological parameter perfectly
Other observations cannot measure anything about the universe
explanation: Independent probes, such as supernovae, the microwave background and galaxy surveys, constrain cosmological models in different ways. Combining them helps test consistency and uncertainty.

title: A map on the largest scale
question: What is the cosmic web?
choices: The large-scale pattern of filaments, clusters and voids in matter and galaxies
A single galaxy's spiral arm
A literal net placed around the universe
explanation: On very large scales, matter and galaxies form a network of filaments and dense nodes separated by less dense voids. Gravity drives much of this structure's growth.

title: Galaxies and filaments
question: In the cosmic web, where are massive galaxy clusters commonly found?
choices: Only at the center of every void
Only inside the Solar System
At dense intersections of filaments
explanation: Matter tends to gather where filaments intersect. Those dense nodes can host galaxy groups and clusters, while less dense regions form voids.

title: Gaps in the cosmic map
question: What is a cosmic void?
choices: A black hole's event horizon
A large region with a lower density of galaxies and matter than its surroundings
A region guaranteed to contain absolutely no particles
explanation: Cosmic voids are relatively underdense regions within large-scale structure. They are not necessarily perfectly empty and should not be confused with black holes.

title: From smooth to web
question: How did small early density differences become large-scale structure in standard models?
choices: Gravity amplified differences over time
Gravity made every region exactly identical
Galaxies were fully formed at the CMB epoch
explanation: Slightly denser regions attracted more matter through gravity, helping early differences grow into galaxies, clusters and filaments over cosmic time.

title: A galactic neighborhood
question: What is a galaxy group?
choices: A group of planets around a single star
A single star and its moons
A collection of galaxies associated by gravity
explanation: A galaxy group contains multiple galaxies in a shared gravitational environment. The Milky Way and Andromeda belong to the Local Group.

title: A larger assembly
question: What distinguishes a galaxy cluster from a single galaxy?
choices: A cluster has no gravitational mass
A cluster contains many galaxies together with gas and dark matter
A cluster is one star with many planets
explanation: Galaxy clusters contain many galaxies, hot gas and substantial dark matter. They are large gravitational structures rather than individual galaxies.

title: A galaxy in view
question: What is characteristic of a spiral galaxy?
choices: A disk with a spiral pattern
Every star lies on one straight line
It contains no gas or dust
explanation: Spiral galaxies have disks with spiral structures and typically contain stars, gas and dust. The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy, viewed from within its disk.

title: Two galaxies nearby
question: Can galaxies merge over cosmic time?
choices: No: galaxies can never interact
Yes, but only if their individual stars all collide
Yes: gravity can bring galaxies together and reshape them
explanation: Galaxies can interact and merge under gravity, changing their shapes and redistributing gas and stars. Individual stellar collisions are comparatively unlikely.

title: A cluster beyond visible light
question: Why are X-ray observations useful for studying galaxy clusters?
choices: They make gravitational lensing disappear
They reveal very hot gas between galaxies
They show only Earth's atmosphere
explanation: Galaxy clusters contain large amounts of hot intracluster gas that emits X-rays. X-ray observations reveal material that ordinary visible-light images do not show as clearly.

title: A simulated cosmic web
question: When a visualization colors filaments in a cosmic-web simulation, what should a viewer remember?
choices: The colors illustrate modeled matter and are not necessarily what eyes would see
Every colored filament is an ordinary visible-light photograph
The simulation is a literal picture of the entire universe
explanation: Cosmic-web visualizations often use color to represent simulated or inferred matter. The colors communicate the model; they are not necessarily the scene's natural visual appearance.

title: A star begins
question: Where do stars form?
choices: In dense regions of gas and dust clouds
In completely empty space without matter
Only inside existing planets
explanation: Stars form when dense regions in molecular clouds collapse under gravity. The collapsing material heats up and can develop into a protostar before sustained core fusion begins.

title: When a star switches on
question: What marks the beginning of a star's main-sequence life?
choices: The first formation of any dust
The end of all gravitational attraction
Sustained hydrogen fusion in its core
explanation: A main-sequence star sustains hydrogen fusion in its core. The energy released supports the hot star against gravitational collapse for a long period.

title: A long-lived balance
question: What helps support a main-sequence star against gravity?
choices: Cosmic expansion inside its core
Pressure associated with the hot gas and energy generated by fusion
A solid surface around the star
explanation: In a main-sequence star, gravity pulls inward while pressure in the hot stellar material provides support. Fusion replenishes energy and helps maintain this balance.

title: A bigger star's clock
question: How does a very massive star's lifetime generally compare with that of a low-mass star?
choices: It is shorter because it uses fuel much faster
It is always longer because it starts with more fuel
Every star has exactly the same lifetime
explanation: Massive stars have more fuel but consume it at a much higher rate. Their lives are generally much shorter than those of low-mass stars.

title: Our Sun's later chapter
question: What is the Sun expected to become after its main-sequence phase?
choices: A supernova immediately
A new galaxy
A red giant
explanation: After exhausting hydrogen in its core, the Sun is expected to expand into a red giant. Later, its outer layers will be shed and its core will remain as a white dwarf.

title: A cooling stellar remnant
question: What is a white dwarf?
choices: A planet made only of light
The compact remnant core of a star such as the Sun after outer layers are shed
A newly formed galaxy
explanation: A white dwarf is the exposed compact core left after a low- or intermediate-mass star sheds its outer layers. It gradually cools over a very long time.

title: A dramatic ending
question: What can happen near the end of a massive star's life?
choices: Its core can collapse and trigger a supernova
It always becomes a planet without changing
It stops obeying gravity
explanation: A sufficiently massive star can undergo core collapse, producing a supernova. The outcome depends on the star's properties and can leave a compact remnant.

title: A dense remnant
question: What can remain after some massive stars explode?
choices: A new Solar System immediately
Only an empty space with no matter
A neutron star
explanation: Some core-collapse supernovae leave neutron stars, extremely dense compact remnants. Other outcomes, including black holes, depend on the mass and physics of the collapse.

title: A boundary around a black hole
question: What is an event horizon?
choices: The edge of the observable universe
A boundary beyond which light cannot escape to distant observers
A solid glowing surface of ordinary matter
explanation: A black hole's event horizon is the boundary of the region from which signals cannot escape to distant observers. It should not be pictured as an ordinary solid surface.

title: The universe's ingredients
question: Where were many elements heavier than helium produced?
choices: In stars and stellar explosions or related events
Only in Earth's atmosphere
All in their present amounts during the first minutes
explanation: Stars make many heavier elements through nuclear reactions, and stellar explosions or related events distribute material into space. The early universe mainly produced the lightest nuclei.

title: A calibrated light
question: How can a standard candle help estimate an astronomical distance?
choices: Compare its calibrated intrinsic brightness with its observed brightness
Assume all objects have identical brightness
Measure only its color without any calibration

They never change brightness
Their pulsation period relates to their intrinsic luminosity
